What Is Conversion Rate Optimization, and When to Do It

By lowob · 5 June 2026 · Updated 10 November 2026 · 4-minute read · Growth / Conversion

Your website is attracting visitors, but too few are signing up, booking a call or completing an application. Before spending more money bringing people in, it makes sense to ask what is stopping the people already there.

That is the job of conversion rate optimization, usually called CRO. It means finding problems in the path from visitor to useful action, making a change for a reason and checking whether that change helped.

CRO is not just changing the button color

A typical process is simple: look at where visitors leave, talk to customers or review support questions, form a hypothesis and test a specific improvement. You might simplify an application, explain a confusing fee or make the next step clearer on a mobile screen.

A new design can help, but a prettier page is not proof of better conversion. Neither is a temporary spike in sign-ups after a small edit.

Optimize the action the business actually needs

Imagine a hypothetical fintech app whose landing page converts more visitors into sign-ups after a redesign. That looks promising until the team discovers that fewer of those users actually fund their accounts.

If the business earns revenue from active funded customers, the important measure cannot stop at registration. Look at the steps in between: qualifying interest, completing identity checks, funding the account and using the product again.

The right conversion depends on the business. An enterprise software company may care about qualified demos. A developer platform may care about successful integrations. A commerce company may care about completed purchases that are not immediately refunded.

Attract

Are the visitors looking for a problem this product solves?

Activate

Can they understand the offer and complete the next meaningful step?

Retain

Do those new customers continue to use the product or reach the intended outcome?

Look for confusion before assuming people need persuasion

Start with analytics that show the path through the product. Pair those numbers with what users actually report. Do support tickets repeatedly mention unclear pricing? Do people abandon a form when asked for identity documents? Is the mobile page too slow to use?

For a regulated product, explain why personal information is required and what happens next. Make fees, eligibility and important conditions easy to understand. Improving clarity can reduce wasted applications as well as increase qualified conversions.

A useful hypothesis is specific: “Applicants may leave at the identity-check step because the page does not explain why the information is needed.” That is easier to investigate than “the landing page needs to convert better.”

Use A/B tests when you have enough information

An A/B test compares different experiences to see whether a change improves an outcome. Good tests need an appropriate sample size and a measurement plan chosen before the team looks at the results.

A page converting at 3% may need thousands of visits per variation to detect a modest lift reliably, depending on the effect size and statistical method. Use a sample-size calculator for the actual assumptions instead of declaring a winner after a few dozen visits. Optimizely also describes how statistical thresholds affect the time and data needed to reach a conclusion.

Be cautious about changing the rules mid-test or checking for a winner every day without a method designed for repeated looks. If a test is inconclusive, say so and use the learning to refine the next hypothesis.

CRO cannot fix the wrong audience

If almost nobody visits a page, the team may not have enough data for a meaningful A/B test. It can still improve confusing forms, missing disclosures or broken mobile layouts through observation and usability review. Those are sensible fixes, just not statistically proven conversion lifts.

If most visitors were never likely to buy, fix the audience, offer or acquisition channel first. Conversion work is powerful when qualified people encounter unnecessary friction. It cannot turn completely irrelevant traffic into customers.

lowob takeaways

  • Find the blocker. Investigate what confuses or stops suitable visitors before redesigning.
  • Use the right success metric. Registrations matter less than the actions that create real customer value.
  • Be honest about evidence. A/B tests need enough data; observation is useful but different.
  • Fix acquisition when necessary. CRO cannot rescue a page filled with the wrong audience.

Sources and notes
